tip: 'Achar que' is the casual Brazilian way to say 'to think that.' It's much more common than 'pensar que' in everyday speech.
'Saber' + infinitive = to know how to do something. 'Saber cozinhar' = to know how to cook.
'Num/numa' are contractions of 'em + um/uma.' They're standard in both speech and writing.
'Ser' for professions: 'ela é médica.' Portuguese normally skips the article between 'ser' and the profession.
'Dar uma olhada' means 'to take a look.' Brazilians love using 'dar uma' + noun for quick actions: 'dar uma ligada' (make a quick call), 'dar uma volta' (take a walk).
'Num' is 'em' plus 'um' squeezed together: 'num apartamento' means 'in an apartment'.
In Brazil, 'arroz e feijão' is the staple daily meal – you'll hear this combination constantly.
'Todo' + a singular noun with no article means every: 'todo verão' (every summer). Add the article, 'todo o verão', and it means the whole summer.
The diminutive '-inho/-inha' is extremely common in Brazilian Portuguese. 'Café' adds a linking 'z': 'cafezinho' (little coffee) is a cultural institution, offered practically everywhere.
Use 'ser' for permanent locations of buildings and places. The restaurant won't move – 'é no centro.'
'Estar' marks a state happening right now: 'está ocupada agora' says she is busy at this moment, not by nature.
'Andar de' + vehicle means to ride/go by: 'andar de bicicleta', 'andar de ônibus', 'andar de carro'.
'Conhecer' means to get to know or visit for the first time. 'A gente quer conhecer o Rio' = we want to visit/experience Rio.
'Ter sorte' means 'to be lucky' – literally 'to have luck.' Another 'ter' expression where English uses 'to be.'
'Ter razão' means 'to be right' – another case where Portuguese uses 'ter' (have) where English uses 'to be.'
'Estar' + the '-ndo' form emphasizes the temporary nature: 'estou morando' = I'm living (for now, temporarily), not permanently.
'Pão de queijo' is a beloved Brazilian snack – small cheese bread rolls made with tapioca flour. Found at nearly every bakery and café.
'Café da manhã' is the Brazilian term for breakfast. In Portugal, they say 'pequeno-almoço.'
In Brazilian Portuguese, 'ônibus' is the word for bus. In Portugal, they say 'autocarro.'
'Aproveitamos o feriado' uses 'aproveitar', 'make the most of'. On its own, 'aproveita' is Brazil's everyday way to say 'enjoy'.
'Vêm' (with circumflex) is the 'vocês'/'eles' form of 'vir' (to come). Don't confuse it with 'veem' from 'ver' (to see).
'Todo sábado' without the article means 'every Saturday.' With the article, 'todo o sábado' usually means 'the whole Saturday' instead.
'Há' + time period expresses duration in the present: 'moro no Brasil há três anos' = I've been living in Brazil for three years.
'A gente' is informal for 'nós' and takes the same verb form as 'ele/ela': 'a gente corre', not 'a gente corremos.'
'Combinar de' + infinitive is how Brazilians say 'to make plans to' or 'to arrange to' do something.
Scheduled events use 'ser': 'a reunião é às três.' Times and dates normally use 'ser' too.
'Ser' is for permanent traits like nationality and identity. 'Sou brasileiro' – it's who you are, not a temporary state.
The soup isn't permanently cold – it became cold: 'está fria'. Use 'estar' for changeable conditions of objects.
Yes/no questions keep statement word order: 'vocês usam o metrô' stays put and rising intonation alone turns it into a question.
'Ir' plus an infinitive is the spoken future: 'vai começar' means 'he is going to start'. It outpaces the one-word future tense in speech.
